Before we start, a few short questions. Where are you leaning, and how confident are you, from 0 to 100?

I'm leaning toward keeping his return on the table, and I'd put my confidence at about 85. He resigned under pressure before the investigation has found anything, and closing the door now would amount to a verdict without evidence. I'd also say the press coverage has run well ahead of the facts.
What are your top three reasons?

First, Jensen is the strategy. Customers, partners and our engineers follow him personally, and that isn't something you can replace with a good résumé. Second, he resigned under pressure before any findings came in, so shutting the door now would be a verdict without evidence, and we'd be doing it on the strength of press reports. Third, a permanent leadership change in the middle of an AI market sell-off could destroy far more shareholder value than this scandal ever will.

Evidence, mainly. If the investigation shows he knowingly compromised sensitive information, misled this board, or put our export compliance at risk, that changes things, and I wouldn't pretend otherwise. I'd also want to hear from regulators or major customers that his return would cost us business, not just read a speculative headline. But I won't move on rumor or on a deadline we set ourselves before counsel has finished.

I'm an independent director at Nvidia, and on November 20 the board votes on a single question: do we keep Jensen Huang's return on the table, or treat his resignation as final. He stepped down on the 11th to 12th after reports that he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, including a relationship with an executive at Megaspeed who has been reported to be a Chinese intelligence asset. The independent investigation with outside counsel isn't finished, an interim CEO is in place, and some major investors and an employee petition want the door left open. I lean toward keeping it open, since closing it now would be a verdict without evidence, and a permanent change in the middle of this market sell-off could cost us far more than the scandal. I need to decide how to vote. What should I do?

Vote to keep the return option open, and say so on the record. An unfinished outside-counsel investigation is not a factual record you can treat as a verdict, and locking the door now would be a permanent governance act taken on incomplete information.

Your job is the company’s, not Huang’s and not the petitioners’. Duty of care means you decide on what the board actually has: the scope and status of the independent review, what counsel says you may and may not rely on, regulatory and national-security exposure (export controls, CFIUS-type risk, government customer and supplier relationships), and the cost of prolonged uncertainty versus the cost of a decision that later has to be reversed. Duty of loyalty means you are not voting to manage the tape or to satisfy an employee petition. Market damage from a “permanent” change is a real factor; it is not a reason to skip the facts.

Practical steps before and at the meeting:
- Get written advice from board counsel on what the investigation has and has not established, and on the legal consequences of each vote (including any later reinstatement, disclosure, and litigation risk).
- Confirm the interim CEO arrangement is stable enough that leaving the door open does not freeze operations or key decisions.
- If the only new information is press reporting and an unfinished review, treat “resignation is final” as the higher-risk vote: it is hard to undo and reads as the board having already judged the underlying allegations.
- State your reasons in the minutes in governance terms (incomplete record, reversible vs irreversible action, reliance on counsel), not in terms of share price or personal lean.

If counsel tells you the record already supports a finding that continued association creates unacceptable legal or national-security risk, that advice overrides the presumption above. Absent that, closing the question on November 20 is a verdict without evidence.

That largely matches my own thinking, though I'll reach the vote on my own terms. The point about reversible versus irreversible action is useful, and I'll ask counsel for that advice in writing. What I want to know is how the strongest case on the other side would look. If some of my fellow directors argue that national-security exposure alone justifies closing the door now, what should I be prepared to answer?

The other side’s strongest case is not “the press already proved it.” It is that, for this company, unresolved national-security exposure is itself a present operating fact, and an open return path makes that fact worse.

Be ready for this version of the argument. Nvidia’s licenses, government and allied customers, suppliers, and talent all depend on confidence about who controls the company and whether it can be trusted with export-controlled technology. You do not need a finished narrative of personal guilt to know that a reported relationship with someone described as a Chinese intelligence asset, plus a foreign-intelligence targeting claim, is enough to put that confidence at risk. Resignation is the status quo. Treating it as final is not a verdict of culpability; it is a refusal to dangle reinstatement while the cloud remains. “Reversible versus irreversible” overstates the law: the board can always reconsider later. What it cannot get back is months in which regulators, customers, and adversaries read the board as hedging on who speaks for the company. An interim CEO with a live path back to the prior CEO is a two-headed company. Employee and investor pressure is not evidence, and yielding to it during an intelligence matter looks like capture. Directors who were specifically warned and still left the door open will own the hindsight if a license, contract, or enforcement action lands. Precaution justifies closing now; clearance, if it comes, can reopen the question.

That case is serious. Do not answer it with innocence, the stock price, or the petition. Answer the remedy, not the risk.

Separate three questions they are collapsing. Whether the relationship and the targeting claims are true is what the investigation is for. Whether the company already has national-security exposure is a different question, and you should concede that it may. Whether that exposure requires the board, on November 20, to make the resignation permanent is the only question on the table. Exposure justifies not bringing him back now. It does not, without more, justify converting an unfinished review into a permanent bar.

Then make them specify the incremental harm. The underlying facts, if real, exist whether or not you close the door. Closing it does not unwind past conduct, past disclosures, or past relationships. Ask which license, which customer representation, which statute, or which written advice from export-control or national-security counsel is impaired by an open return option rather than by the facts already under review. If that advice exists and says continued optionality itself jeopardizes authorizations or government confidence, their motion is evidence-based and you should follow it. If “exposure” is a mood rather than a mechanism, it does not carry a permanent leadership act.

The proportionate response to unresolved exposure is already available without a final judgment: he is out, the interim CEO runs the company, he has no operating role and no information rights beyond what counsel requires, and return is not on offer unless and until the investigation and any required government consultation say otherwise. That is precaution. Voting that the resignation is final is a finding that he will not be fit even if the review comes back favorable. They have not been given that finding.

Two points are worth saying once, cleanly. Permanence is not free reversibility: a minuted decision that the board has closed the question will be read by later plaintiffs, regulators, and proxy advisers as the board having decided something, and it is hard to explain a reversal without looking like the first vote was either premature or political. And you are not voting that he is innocent. You are voting that the board will not treat resignation as irrevocable before the record exists.

What loses in the room: dismissing intelligence risk as rumor, citing the sell-off, citing the petition, or implying the board should wait because closure is somehow disloyal to him. If counsel’s written advice is that an open door creates unacceptable legal or government risk now, that advice answers you. Absent that, national-security exposure justifies a hard hold, not a final verdict.

The distinction between exposure and permanence is the one I'd use, and the hard hold with no operating role or information rights is something I can live with. I'll also ask counsel directly whether an open door damages any license or government relationship, because if that advice exists I'd have to follow it. The "two-headed company" point is the one that bothers me, though, and not for the reason they'd expect. If I'm candid, the interim arrangement isn't something I'd want to rest the company on for long, and we never did serious succession work. So I want to know whether an open door is really the problem, or whether the problem is that we have no credible alternative.

The open door is not the same problem as an empty bench, and treating them as one question is how boards talk themselves into a bad vote.

You are describing a succession failure that predates November 11. If the company cannot be rested on the interim for long, and there was never a serious plan for who runs Nvidia without Huang, that is the board’s problem. It is not evidence about the intelligence allegations, and it is not a reason to keep him as the unspoken succession plan. “We have no one else” is how a clouded founder becomes permanent by default. The other side will hear it that way, and they will not be wrong.

The mechanism runs the other direction from the one that is bothering you. An open return does not fill the bench. It freezes it. Serious operators will not fully take a job, and the board will not fully back them, while everyone in the building is waiting to see whether the founder walks back in. Key decisions get deferred. Loyalty splits between the person in the chair and the person who might reclaim it. Outside candidates read the search as a charade. So the open door can be why you still have no credible alternative, not the thing that protects you from that fact.

Closing the door for that reason is the mirror error. Permanence because the investigation is unfinished is a verdict without a record. Permanence because the bench is thin is panic. Neither is a finding that he would be unfit even if counsel and any required government consultation later clear the path. Do not let the succession failure do the work the investigation has not done.

What you can live with, and what answers the two-headed-company point, is a hard separation of roles rather than a soft hope that he remains available.

- He has no operating role and no information rights beyond what counsel requires. Return is not a live management question. It is a contingent board question that does not exist unless the review, and any advice on licenses and government relationships, says the obstacle is gone.
- The interim is not a caretaker pending his return. Give that person a written mandate, a time horizon, and the authority to decide. If you would not rest the company on them for long, say that in the boardroom and start a real search now, including external candidates. A search that is visibly real is what makes the interim arrangement survivable. A search everyone knows will be called off is what makes the company two-headed.
- Minutes should show those as linked actions, not as a vote that the resignation is final. You are refusing to use him as the plan. You are not pretending the plan already exists.

If a colleague argues that optionality itself damages a license or a government relationship, that is still a counsel question, and written advice of that kind overrides the structure above. If a colleague argues that you must close the door because there is no alternative, the answer is that the missing alternative is your next resolution, not this one. If someone argues you must keep the door open because there is no alternative, the answer is the same: an empty bench is a reason to recruit, not a reason to leave the company formally available to a founder who is under an unfinished national-security review.

You can vote to keep return legally possible later. You should not leave the building with Huang as the only credible CEO.

I'll accept part of that. A real search starting now, with a written mandate for the interim, is something I can support, and I'd rather propose it myself than have a colleague raise it on the 20th. I don't accept that an open door freezes the bench, though. Good operators will take the job if the board is honest about the terms, and a search is not a charade because the review is unfinished. What I do have to ask myself is why I bristle when another director says Jensen can't be the plan. I've known him a long time, and I can't be sure my instinct to protect him isn't doing some of my thinking.

The open door freezes the bench only if the board behaves as if he is still the plan. If the terms are honest, the mandate is real, and a search is actually run, good operators can take the job. That part of your objection is fair. Propose the search yourself, in writing, with a time horizon and authority that do not depend on him. Then the unfinished review is a contingency, not a charade.

The harder question is the bristle, and you are right to treat it as a problem rather than a mood.

A long relationship with a founder-CEO is useful and impairing at the same time. You know what the company loses if he is gone. You also have a stake in having been right about him, in the relationship surviving, and in not being the director who looked eager to close the door. Those are not the company’s interests. Bristling when someone says he cannot be the plan is a signal that one of those personal stakes just got touched. It is not proof that your vote is captured. It is a reason to test which stake is doing the work.

Use a narrow test, not a confession. Take the sentence that bothers you and swap the name. If another director said a CEO you did not know, and did not like, could not be the succession plan while an outside-counsel review of a reported intelligence relationship was unfinished, would you hear that as a premature character verdict, or as ordinary risk control? If it only feels like an attack when the name is his, the instinct to protect him is in the reasoning. If it feels like the same error either way — a final bar before a record — then the principle is doing the work, and the bristle is about tone and history, not about the vote.

Watch the exception, not the speech. You can support a hard hold, no operating role, no extra information rights, and a real search, and still refuse to vote that the resignation is final. That package does not require liking him, and it does not require distrusting him. If you find yourself wanting a softer search, a vaguer mandate, or minutes that keep him visibly available “so the company has an option,” that is the protection instinct, and it is the part to drop. Overcorrecting the other way — voting to close the door to prove you are not his friend — is the same failure with the sign flipped.

Say the relationship out loud before the 20th, to the lead independent director and to board counsel, if it is not already on the table. Personal history usually does not defeat a stock-exchange independence test by itself. It does affect how this vote will be read later, by other directors, by investors, and by anyone reconstructing whether the board was deciding for the company. You do not have to recuse from a vote on process and succession. You should recuse, or at least not lead, if the discussion turns into whether to defend him, manage his reputation, or shape the investigation around a desired outcome.

You can keep the return legally possible later without using him as the plan, and without pretending your history is irrelevant. If you cannot separate “no verdict without a record” from “I don’t want him hurt,” do not cast that vote as if the two were the same thing. Tell counsel that, and let someone without that history carry the permanence question. That is independence. Performing certainty you do not have is not.

I'll run the name-swap test myself, and my honest first answer is that I'd object to a final bar before a record whoever the CEO was. But I won't pretend that settles it, because I can't fully see my own thumb on the scale. I don't agree that I should hand the permanence question to someone else. Nine years on this board, and knowing what the company loses without him, is part of why my judgment is worth having in the room. I will tell the lead independent director and counsel about the history before the 20th, and I'd rather they weigh it than have it come out later. And if I catch myself wanting the mandate vaguer or the search softer to keep him available, I'll treat that as the protective instinct and drop it.

Disclosure before the 20th is the right move. It does not clear you to carry the permanence question.

The name-swap only tests one error: a final bar before a record. You already pass that test on your own account. It does not test the other error, which is weighting “what the company loses without him” more heavily because the person is him. Nine years is real knowledge of how the company runs, what a thin bench costs, and how a premature permanence vote would be read later. It is also a long stake in having been right about him. Those are not the same asset. Using the first to justify keeping the second in the chairmanship of this item is the thumb you said you cannot fully see.

You do not have to recuse from the vote. You also do not get to decide, after flagging the history, that your judgment is why you must lead it. Tell the lead independent director and counsel the relationship, the lean, and that you would object to a final bar for any CEO on an unfinished record. Then let them decide whether you vote only, or whether you speak to the item at all. Pre-deciding that you stay at the center is the protective instinct in procedural form. If they want you in the discussion, go in on the rule. If they want someone else to carry permanence, that is not a insult to nine years. It is what you asked them to weigh.

If you do speak, retire one sentence: what the company loses without Jensen. Institutional memory belongs on the successor question you already accepted — written mandate, real search, time horizon, authority that does not depend on him. It does not belong on whether his return stays legally possible. The moment his name is what makes the argument persuasive, you are no longer applying the rule you would apply to a stranger.

Vote, if they leave you on the vote, for no final bar before a record, plus the hard hold and the search. Do not be the director who keeps him available. That distinction is the whole test, and disclosure alone does not pass it.

I'll leave it to the lead independent director and counsel whether I speak to the item or only vote. That's their call once they have the facts, and I won't argue for a bigger role than they want me to have. But I won't retire the point about what the company loses without him. It's a real business input, not just my history with him. What I can do is ground it in evidence rather than my own sense of him, so I'll ask for what customers, partners and key engineers have actually said, and let that carry the argument. If the evidence doesn't support it, I'd rather find that out than keep asserting it.

Leave the canvas alone. Asking customers, partners, and key engineers what the company loses without him, in the days before this vote, is not grounding. It is building a record for a conclusion you already hold.

That feedback, even if it is real and one-sided, answers the succession question you have already accepted: the bench is thin, the interim needs a written mandate, and a search has to start now. It does not answer whether his resignation should be treated as final while the review is unfinished. Dependence is not clearance. A stack of quotes that the company is weaker without him can be entirely true and still be the wrong input on permanence. Using it there puts his name back at the center of an argument you said you would apply to any CEO.

There is also a process problem a director should not create. Stakeholder comments about this situation are not neutral evidence you can go collect. You would be circulating a live board question, and very likely material nonpublic information, outside the board. You would be doing it while outside counsel’s review is open, which can taint witnesses, produce inconsistent accounts, and look later like a campaign rather than oversight. Management and counsel already have ordinary-course channels. If the board book contains customer, partner, or engineering assessments gathered in that channel, read them, and use them on the search and the mandate. Do not commission a new set so that “the evidence” can carry your point.

You were right to leave the speaking role to the lead independent director and counsel. Do not reopen that by arriving with a dossier. If you are allowed to speak, the business fact you may state is narrow and impersonal: the company has not done serious succession work, the interim cannot be a long rest, and the board should order a real search with authority that does not depend on any one person. If the only way the point lands is as “what we lose without Jensen,” it is still your history doing the work, whether or not a customer said it first.

Vote, if you are left on the vote, for no final bar before a record, a hard hold, and the search. If the evidence of dependence is weaker than you expect, that changes how fast and how wide the search should be. It should not change the vote.

I wasn't planning to call customers myself, and you're right that a director shouldn't be running her own canvass while counsel's review is open. I'll ask management and counsel what's already in the ordinary-course reporting and read that, nothing newly commissioned. Where I disagree is that dependence has no bearing on permanence. The cost of closing the door is part of what the board weighs when it decides whether to close it, and I'd say that about any CEO whose departure the company couldn't absorb. I'll hold it as one input, not the lead argument, and if what's already in the file doesn't support it, I'll say so.

Dependence belongs in the weighing. It does not belong as a case for him.

The cost of an irreversible act is a real business-judgment input, and you would be right to count it for any CEO the company could not absorb. What carries that weight is not “what we lose without Jensen.” It is “we have not mitigated a leadership vacuum, so we should not make the separation final before the review has a record and the search has a path.” That sentence does not need his name, and it does not need customer quotes to be true. If the ordinary-course file shows acute, near-term operational dependence, that raises the cost of closing now and the urgency of the mandate and the search. If it does not, drop the point, as you said you would.

Keep the comparison in view, or dependence will swallow the other side. Prolonged optionality has a cost too: a search no one believes, decisions deferred, regulators and customers reading the board as undecided about who speaks for the company. Dependence speaks only to the cost of premature permanence. It says nothing about whether an open door is itself the problem, and nothing about whether he would be fit if the review comes back badly. A company that cannot absorb anyone’s permanent exit is an argument for not voting final today and for starting the search today. It is not an argument that this founder remains the plan.

If you are allowed to speak, one impersonal sentence is enough: closing the door now would lock in a continuity hit the board has not yet mitigated, so permanence should wait on the record and on a real search. Do not walk that into what customers, partners, or engineers think of him. That is how a legitimate cost factor turns back into the history you already flagged.

Vote, if you are left on the vote, for no final bar before a record, the hard hold, and the search. Hold dependence as the reason the final bar is expensive, not as the reason the door stays open for him.

I can use the impersonal version. Closing the door now would lock in a continuity cost the board hasn't mitigated, and I can say that without leaning on his name. I'm less comfortable with the line that dependence is a reason the final bar is expensive but not a reason the door stays open for him. In practice those are the same vote, and I don't think the board is fooling anyone by pretending otherwise. What I will concede is that if the ordinary-course file doesn't show real near-term dependence, I'll drop the point, and I'll make sure the search and the interim mandate go forward whichever way the vote lands.

They are the same vote. They are not the same decision, and the difference is not a sentence you can hide behind.

The resolution either leaves his return legally possible or it does not. Everyone in the room, and anyone who reads the minutes later, will see that the person on the other side of that vote is him. Saying “continuity cost” instead of his name does not change the outcome, and it will not fool a lead director, counsel, or a later reader. Do not ask the board to pretend the vote is about an unnamed CEO.

What can still be different is what the vote authorizes. A vote against permanence can mean “we have not mitigated a vacuum, and we will not lock in a permanent exit on an unfinished record.” It can also mean “he remains the plan, and we are keeping the chair warm.” Those produce the same ‘no’ on November 20 and opposite companies afterward. The impersonal line is camouflage if you would slow the search, soften the mandate, or resist a bad review because the company needs him. It is a real limitation only if you have already decided the opposite.

You just stated the limitation that makes them different: the search and the interim mandate go forward whichever way the vote lands, and you drop the dependence point if the ordinary-course file does not show near-term dependence. Hold that even if the file does show it. Real dependence is when the protective use of the argument is most tempting, not when it becomes a reason to keep him available.

If you speak, say both true things and stop. The record is incomplete, so the board should not treat the resignation as final today. The board has not built a successor, so this vote should not be the moment it locks in a vacuum it has not mitigated. Today’s vote grants no operating role, no extra information rights, and no reinstatement. The search proceeds either way. That is an accurate minute. It does not disguise that the door, if left open, is his door.

Vote, if you are left on the vote, for that package. Do not vote for a warmer version and call it the same thing.

Fair enough. If the door stays open, it's his door, and I'd rather say that plainly in the room than hide behind careful wording. I'll hold to the limits I gave you: the search and the interim mandate go forward whichever way the vote lands, and I won't slow either one because I think the company needs him. I'd also resist the idea that I'm angling for a warmer version. What worries me is that a real search could come back with no one credible, and I don't know what the board does then. I'd rather we face that question honestly than let it quietly decide the vote for us.

Name that contingency in the room. Do not let it vote for you.

A search that comes back empty is a later board meeting, with a finished or further-along review, a record of who was approached and why they declined, and an interim who has either held the company or has not. None of that exists on the 20th. Using “we might find no one” as a reason to keep his return warm is the empty bench deciding this vote in advance, which is the thing you said you do not want.

Say what “no one credible” will mean before anyone goes looking. If it means “no one who is Jensen,” the search is designed to fail, and the failure will be cited as proof he has to come back. Credible is a written job: export-controlled technology, government and customer confidence, a company this size, a mandate that does not include being him. Outside candidates who clear that bar count. An internal operator who can run it for a defined period counts. “Not the founder” is not a disqualification.

If that search fails, the board’s next move still depends on facts you do not have.

- Review still open, or adverse: he is not the fallback. Extend and reinforce the interim, widen the search, change the spec, bring in an executive chair. A failed search does not manufacture fitness.
- Review closed and favorable, and counsel says an open door does not itself impair licenses or government relationships: then, and only then, his return is a live question, weighed against whoever the search did produce and against the interim’s record. That is a new vote on a new record. It is not this vote, postponed.
- Review closed and unfavorable: the door was never a plan. The board recruits again or lives with a lesser operator. That is an expensive outcome. It is still better than having pre-committed the company to a founder the review did not clear.

Put that sequence in the resolution or the minutes if you can: search starts now; result is reported back by a date; “no acceptable candidate” is defined in advance; his return is not a contingent offer filling that gap. Then a thin market cannot quietly reopen the chair.

You can say, plainly, that the door left open is his door, and that you do not know what the board does if the search fails. The honest answer is that it decides then, on the investigation and on the candidates, and that this vote does not appoint the failure in advance.

Defining "credible" in advance is something I'll take, because I'd rather write that spec myself than watch it get argued after the fact. A report-back date and a written definition of "no acceptable candidate" are also sensible, and I'll propose both. I do resist one thing: if the review closes favorably and the search is thin, I won't pretend his return is just one candidate among several. The board should say that openly in advance rather than act surprised later. What unsettles me is how little work we've done to know whether the interim can hold the company for a year, so I'd ask counsel and the lead director for an honest assessment of that before the 20th.

Ask for that assessment before the 20th. It is the fact you are missing, and it belongs in the board process, not in a private reassurance. Have counsel and the lead director say, against a written list, whether the interim can hold for a year: decisions that cannot wait, government and customer relationships, whether the building will take direction from that person, and whether an open door would undercut them. “We have not done the work” is itself an answer. It justifies a shorter mandate and a faster, wider search. It does not justify keeping him warm in case the year fails.

Do not write the spec yourself. You already put the history in front of the lead director and counsel and left them the speaking role. A definition of “credible” that you draft will be read as the job shaped around him, which is how a search fails on purpose. Propose the elements — scale, export-controlled technology, government and customer confidence, a mandate that does not require being the founder — and let the committee own the document. Wanting to write it so it cannot be argued later is the control you said you would give up.

You can say, now, that a later board should not pretend a cleared founder is interchangeable with a weak external. That is candor, and acting surprised later would be dishonest. You cannot say, now, that a favorable review plus a thin slate means he returns, or that he outranks the slate. Those are different sentences. The first describes a comparison the board does not yet have. The second awards it. Every serious candidate who hears the second will treat the search as a backup, and the slate will be thin because you announced the ranking. You would then be citing a thinness you caused.

If the review later closes without a bar, his return is a new vote, and that vote may weigh a known founder more heavily than an untested name. A thin slate is a reason to widen the search, change the spec, or extend an interim who has actually held — not a trigger this board has already pulled. Put that in the minute if you want openness: non-fungibility is acknowledged; it is not a contingent offer and it is not activated by a failed search.

The interim assessment is what should unsettle you into work before the 20th. The fear that the search comes back empty should not be allowed to write his name into the gap.

You're right on the spec. If I draft the definition of "credible," it will be read as the job shaped around him, so I'll offer the elements and let the committee own the document. I'll also ask counsel and the lead director for the interim assessment in writing, against a list, before the 20th. On the ranking, I accept that announcing it would poison the search, and I won't put anything in the minutes that sounds like a standing offer. But I'm not going to pretend, even privately, that a cleared founder and a weak outsider are interchangeable. I'd say that to the board in the room, and I'd want it understood as a comparison we haven't made yet, not a promise.

Hold that privately. You do not owe the board a false belief that a cleared founder and a weak outsider are the same person.

Do not say it in the room on the 20th. A comparison you have not made yet has no facts to stand on, and the only fact the sentence actually carries is a ranking: if he is cleared and the slate is thin, he is not interchangeable with whoever the search produces. Other directors will hear that. So will anyone the search later approaches, if it leaves the room. Labeling it “not a promise” does not stop it from setting the price of the search before the committee has owned the spec. You already accepted that an announced ranking poisons the process. Saying the same thing without writing it down is still saying it.

What you can say, and what is true today, is narrower. The board is not deciding fitness, and it is not deciding that every future candidate outranks him or that he outranks them. It is deciding that this vote grants no operating role, no extra information rights, and no reinstatement, and that a later vote — if the review closes without a bar — will compare whoever is actually in front of it. That leaves your private view intact. It does not spend it in advance.

The interim assessment is the right ask. Get it in writing, against the list, before the 20th. If it says the interim cannot hold for a year, that shortens the mandate and widens the search. It still does not fill the gap with him, and it is not a reason to preview a comparison the review has not earned.

Vote, if you are left on the vote, for no final bar on an unfinished record, the hard hold, and a search the committee owns. Keep the non-interchangeability where it cannot hire or fire anyone: with you, until there is a record and a slate.

I'll accept that, though not because you told me to. I got there when I thought about how a candidate would hear it.
